translationRepairs: Zhu Ru was greatly terrified and wept.
The dwarfs were greatly terrified and wept.
硃儒 is the collective noun for the court dwarfs, not a personal name; context (s0015 騶硃儒; s0018 硃儒皆) confirms a group, so 'Zhu Ru' is a mistranslation and 'the dwarfs' is correct.
Presently they heard the emperor passing; the Zhu Ru all wailed and knocked their heads.
Presently they heard the emperor passing; the dwarfs all wailed and knocked their heads.
硃儒皆號泣頓首 uses 皆 for the dwarf attendants as a group; treating 硃儒 as the name Zhu Ru invents a person the Chinese does not name.
The Zhu Ru are a little over three feet tall; they receive one sack of grain and two hundred forty cash.
The dwarfs are a little over three feet tall; they receive one sack of grain and two hundred forty cash.
硃儒長三尺餘 continues the same collective dwarf reference contrasted with Shuo's height; 'the dwarfs' restores the sense and 'Zhu Ru' does not.
The Zhu Ru are so stuffed they could die; your servant Shuo is so hungry he could die.
The dwarfs are so stuffed they could die; your servant Shuo is so hungry he could die.
朱儒飽欲死 pairs the dwarfs' satiety with 臣朔飢欲死; the subject is the dwarf group, not a man named Zhu Ru.
He again granted a stone of wine and a hundred jin of meat to take home to the little lord.
He again granted a stone of wine and a hundred jin of meat to take home to his wife.
歸遺細君 means taking the gift home to his wife (細君); 'little lord' invents a wrong referent that the Chinese and the parallel in s0077 do not support.
He would ride out at night and return at dusk with five days' rations, then appear at audience in the Changle Palace—the emperor loved the sport.

At first the emperor slipped out at night and returned the following evening. Later he took provisions for five days, timing his return for court at Changxin Palace. He thoroughly enjoyed these excursions.
會朝長信宮 names Changxin Palace, not Changle, while 後齎五日糧 means that on later excursions he carried five days' provisions.
At that time he went out by night and returned at evening, carrying five days' rations behind him; he would attend court at the Changle Palace— the emperor greatly delighted in it.
At that time he would go out at night and return the following evening. Later he took five days' provisions, returning for court at Changxin Palace; the emperor delighted greatly in these excursions.
The corrected source reads 後齎五日糧 and 長信宮: on later outings he took five days' provisions and returned for court at Changxin Palace.
At first, the emperor's aunt the Princess of Guantao, titled the Grand Dowager Dou's daughter, was married by Marquis of Tangyi Chen Wu.
At first, the emperor's aunt, the Princess of Guantao, was known as Grand Princess Dou and was married to Chen Wu, Marquis of Tangyi.
太主 was the title used for an emperor's aunt and is conventionally rendered Grand Princess. 堂邑侯陳午尚之 means Chen Wu married her, so the revision also corrects the agency and smooths the sentence.

It is as though the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao were your chancellors, Confucius your chief censor, the Grand Duke your commander-in-chief, the Duke of Bi your remonstrating counselor at court, Bian Yanzi your captain of the guard, Gao Yao your chief judge, Hou Ji your minister of agriculture, yiyin day your steward of the palace treasury, Zigong your envoy abroad, Yan Hui and Min Ziqian your court scholars, Zixia your master of rites, Yi your western capital intendant, Zhong You your chief of police, Xie your master of ceremonies for guests, Long Feng your keeper of the imperial genealogy, Boyi your governor of the capital region, Guan Zhong your northern intendant, Lu Ban your chief engineer, Zhong Shanfu your chamberlain for the palace, the Earl of Shen your master of the horse, Prince Jizi of Yanling your keeper of the parks and pools, Baili Xi your commissioner over dependent peoples, Liuxia Hui your chief eunuch, Shi Yu your censor of conduct, Qu Boyu your grand tutor, Kong Fu your tutor to the heir, Sunshu Ao your chief minister to the feudal lords, Zichan your prefect, Wang Qingji your palace gate captain, Xia Yu your ritual cauldron officer, Yi your spearhead guard, and Song Wan your road-clearing escort commander."

Imagine the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao as your chancellors; Confucius as chief censor; the Grand Duke as commander; Duke Bi Gao as court remonstrant; Bian Zhuangzi as captain of the guard; Gao Yao as chief judge; Hou Ji as minister of agriculture; Yi Yin as palace treasurer; Zigong as foreign envoy; Yan Hui and Min Ziqian as court scholars; Zixia as master of rites; Yi as western capital intendant; Zilu as capital commandant; Xie as master of guest ceremonies; Guan Longpeng as keeper of the imperial genealogy; the minister Boyi as metropolitan governor; Guan Zhong as northern capital intendant; Lu Ban as chief engineer; Zhong Shanfu as palace chamberlain; the Earl of Shen as master of the horse; Prince Jizi of Yanling as keeper of parks and waters; Baili Xi as commissioner for dependent peoples; Liuxia Hui as chamberlain to the empress; Shi Yu as censor of conduct; Qu Boyu as grand tutor; Kong Fu as supervisor of the heir apparent's household; Sunshu Ao as chancellor to the feudal lords; Zichan as commandery governor; Prince Qingji as a palace gate guard; Xia Yu as cauldron officer; Yi the Archer as vanguard officer; and Song Wan as road-clearing scout."
The revision restores Yi Yin and normalizes the many historical names and offices in this roster, including Duke Bi Gao, Bian Zhuangzi, Zilu, Guan Longpeng, the minister Boyi, and Prince Qingji.

It is as if you had made the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao your chancellors, Confucius your imperial counselor, the Grand Duke your general, the Duke of Bi, Gao, remonstrator behind the throne; Bian Yanzi as commandant of the guards; Gao Yao as grand judge of trials; Hou Ji as minister of agriculture; yiyin day as minister of the lesser treasury; Zigong sent to foreign states; Yan and Min as erudits; Zixia as Grand Master of ceremonies; Yi as governor of Youfufeng; Jilu as bearer of the golden mace; Xie as grand herald; Long Feng as director of the imperial clan; Boyi as metropolitan governor; Guan Zhong as governor of Fengyi; Lu Ban as superintendent of works; Zhong Shanfu as superintendent of the imperial household; the Earl of Shen as grand coachman; Prince Jizi of Yanling as superintendent of the imperial parks; Baili Xi as director of dependent states; Liuxia Hui as grand director of the palace; Shi Yu as rectifier of conduct; Qu Boyu as grand tutor; Kong Fu as supervisor of the heir apparent; Sunshu Ao as chancellor to the feudal lords; Zichan as commandery governor; Wang Qingji as commander of the palace gates; Xia Yu as cauldron officer; Yi as vanguard chief; Song Wan as marquis who clears the road."

It is as if you had made the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao your chancellors; Confucius your Censor-in-Chief; the Grand Duke your general; Duke Bi Gao your remonstrant at the rear; Bian Zhuangzi your Commandant of the Guards; Gao Yao your Chief Justice; Hou Ji your Minister of Agriculture; Yi Yin your Privy Treasurer; Zigong your envoy abroad; Yan Hui and Min Ziqian your Erudites; Zixia your Minister of Ceremonies; Yi your western capital intendant; Zilu your Capital Commandant; Xie your Grand Herald; Guan Longpeng your Director of the Imperial Clan; the minister Boyi your Metropolitan Governor; Guan Zhong your northern capital intendant; Lu Ban your Superintendent of Works; Zhong Shanfu your Chamberlain for Attendants; the Earl of Shen your Grand Coachman; Prince Jizi of Yanling your Superintendent of Waters and Parks; Baili Xi your Director of Dependent States; Liuxia Hui your Chamberlain for the Empress; Shi Yu your Rectifier; Qu Boyu your Grand Tutor; Kong Fu your supervisor of the heir apparent's household; Sunshu Ao your chancellor to the feudal lords; Zichan your commandery governor; Prince Qingji your Palace Gate Guard; Xia Yu your Cauldron Officer; Yi the Archer your Vanguard Officer; and Song Wan your road-clearing scout."
The literal revision restores Yi Yin and uses the verified normalized names and offices throughout the roster.

The court at that time teemed with talent, and the emperor pressed Shuo again: "Consider Chancellor Gongsun, the Imperial Counselor (name missing in text), Dong Zhongshu, Xiahou Shichang, Sima Xiangru, Wuqiu Shouwang, Zhufu Yan, Zhu Maichen, Yan Zhu, Ji Yan, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan An, Xu Le, Sima Qian, and men of that stamp — all of them learned, articulate, and copious on the page. How do you measure yourself against such company?"

The court at that time teemed with talent, and the emperor pressed Shuo again: "Consider Chancellor Gongsun Hong, Censor-in-Chief Er Kuan, Dong Zhongshu, Xiahou Shichang, Sima Xiangru, Wuqiu Shouwang, Zhufu Yan, Zhu Maichen, Yan Zhu, Ji An, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan An, Xu Le, Sima Qian, and men of that stamp. They are learned, articulate, and prolific writers. How do you measure yourself against such company?"
The source names 公孫弘, 兒大夫 (Er Kuan in his office), and 汲黯; the revision restores all three names and removes the false lacuna.

At this time the court had many worthy talents, and the emperor again asked Shuo: "At present Chancellor Gongsun, the Imperial Counselor (lacuna) grandee, Dong Zhongshu, Xiahou Shichang, Sima Xiangru, Wuqiu Shouwang, Zhufu Yan, Zhu Maichen, Yan Zhu, Ji Yan, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan An, Xu Le, Sima Qian, and their like — all are eloquent, wise, broad, and accomplished, overflowing in literary phrasing; in your own view, sir, how do you compare with them?"

At this time the court had many worthy talents, and the emperor again asked Shuo: "At present Chancellor Gongsun Hong, Censor-in-Chief Er Kuan, Dong Zhongshu, Xiahou Shichang, Sima Xiangru, Wuqiu Shouwang, Zhufu Yan, Zhu Maichen, Yan Zhu, Ji An, Jiao Cang, Zhong Jun, Yan An, Xu Le, Sima Qian, and their like are all eloquent, learned, broad-minded, accomplished, and overflowing in literary expression. In your own view, sir, how do you compare with them?"
The corrected source has 兒大夫, not a lacuna, and names Er Kuan alongside Gongsun Hong and Ji An.

That is why yiyin day swallowed humiliation, shouldered the kitchen cauldron, and seasoned five flavors to win Tang's ear, and the Grand Duke angled on the north bank of the Wei until King Wen found him.

That is why Yi Yin swallowed humiliation, shouldered the kitchen cauldron, and seasoned five flavors to win Tang's ear, and the Grand Duke angled on the north bank of the Wei until King Wen found him.
故伊尹蒙恥辱 names Yi Yin; 'yiyin day' is nonsensical English corruption of that personal name.
Therefore yiyin day bore shame and dishonor, carried cauldron and stand, blended five flavors to seek Tang; the Grand Duke fished on the Wei's north bank (the sunny bank) to see King Wen.
Therefore Yi Yin bore shame and dishonor, carried cauldron and stand, blended five flavors to seek Tang; the Grand Duke fished on the Wei's north bank (the sunny bank) to see King Wen.
The literal likewise must read 伊尹 as Yi Yin rather than 'yiyin day'.
The Grand Duke and yiyin day won such ends; Longpeng and Bigan the other—is that not tragedy?
The Grand Duke and Yi Yin met with such success, while Guan Longpeng and Bigan met with the opposite fate. Is that not tragic?
太公、伊尹 pairs the Grand Duke with Yi Yin, while 龍逢 is the abbreviated name of Guan Longpeng; the revision restores both names and the contrast.
The Grand Duke and yiyin day were thus; Longpeng and Bigan alone were like that—is it not pitiable!
The Grand Duke and Yi Yin fared thus; Guan Longpeng and Bigan alone fared otherwise. Is it not pitiable?
The literal likewise restores Yi Yin and expands the abbreviated 龍逢 to Guan Longpeng.
Could it be that I have failed to understand?"
The doubled 'perhaps' is ungrammatical and 意者寡人殆不明乎 is a self-doubt question. The revision expresses that naturally while retaining the closing quotation mark.
